sections.title: The context
sections.description: Set the foundation for your project: your domain, your users, your goals, and the constraints that shape them. Everything that follows builds on what you define here.

groups.title: Domain
groups.description: Select one or more domains that describe your project. This sets the tone and mechanics for everything that follows.

groups.title: User Profile
groups.description: Describe your user — who they are, what motivates them, and their prior experience with games.

groups.title: Constraints
groups.description: Select the constraints your users or project may face, then add details on any you select.

fields.label: Describe shortly the aim of your software:
Gaming experience
fields.placeholder: e.g., Casual mobile gamers

sections.title: The Experience Timeline
sections.description: Map out how your users' experience evolves over time — from their first interaction to what keeps them coming back. This helps identify where engagement might drop and what should sustain it.

groups.title: Onboarding
groups.description: Describe how new users are introduced to your system for the first time — what they need to learn, and how you'll teach it to them.

groups.title: Re-onboarding
groups.description: Returning users may need a refresher, not a full tutorial. Describe how you'll re-orient them without repeating the full onboarding experience.

groups.title: Updates
groups.description: Define how your system evolves after launch — how frequently you'll release something new, and what that will actually be.

groups.title: Retention anchors
groups.description: Select the mechanisms that keep users emotionally or practically tied to your system, and describe how each one shows up in your design.

groups.title: Drop-out and desistance risks
groups.description: Check any risks that are relevant to your design, so the system can flag where your mechanics may need safeguards.

groups.title: Taxonomy of gamification goals
groups.description: Check the goal types your system uses.

groups.title: Emotional dynamics
groups.description: Rate the expected intensity of each dynamic. High = primary driver. Low = side effect.

fields.label: Outline the main steps and goals of your onboarding:
fields.placeholder: e.g., First 30 seconds: safe tutorial room to practice movement. Tooltips pop up only on first interaction…

fields.label: Outline the main steps and goals of your re-onboarding:
fields.placeholder: e.g., After 14 days of inactivity, show a 'here's what changed' summary. After a major update, highlight only the new feature

fields.title: Content type
fields.hint: Define how your system evolves after launch — how frequently you'll release something new, and what that will actually be.

options.description: Guilds, clans, or alliances that require coordination with others to progress.
Friends, duos, or peer-to-peer obligations — a raid team, a co-op progress bar shared with someone specific.
Habitual touchpoints — daily login, weekly reset, streaks.
Sunk costs — collections, reputation, or progress that feels too painful to abandon.
Public status — cosmetics, leaderboards, titles, avatar personalization.
Unpredictable rewards — loot, drops, or pulls — that keep users coming back for the chance of a rare outcome.
If tasks were to exceed a user's current ability, they could feel overwhelmed and might give up.
If your users hit a wall they can't cross, they lose interest completely — even in goals that matter to them.
If challenges were poorly balanced or overly harsh, users might walk away prematurely.
Relying only on badges and points makes users focus on the rewards instead of the actual goal.
If users can't see how they are doing, they lose direction and drop off.
If a user is stuck too long without hints or boosters, they're much more likely to stop participating.
Completing a specific result or task — finishing a quest or an exploratory mission.
Meeting a standard — earning a set number of points, reaching a level, hitting a leaderboard rank.
Aimed at acquiring new skills or knowledge. In gamification.
These are highly difficult or even potentially impossible goals used to stimulate creative thinking (e.g., achieving 100% completion in a game).
Distal goals are long-term or distant achievements (like completing a whole chapter), while proximal goals are immediate tasks that serve as stepping stones toward the distal objective.
Specific, measurable, attainable, realistic, and time-bound.

fields.label: What do you expect from the system?
Add context the sliders can't capture — what's driving the high ratings, and how you're managing the low ones.

sections.title: Personalization and dynamics
sections.description: Define your user types and how your system adapts to their different motives and goals. Describe what they can shape themselves, what the game adjusts automatically, and what you infer from their behavior.

groups.title: User types
groups.description: Think about your users and what drives them. Understanding their primary motives and matching them to your design mechanics will help you build a system they actually want to use.

groups.title: Dynamics
groups.description: Define how difficulty adapts over time: what signals trigger a change, what actually gets adjusted, and how that adjustment behaves.

options.description: Motivated by purpose — enjoys helping others and sharing knowledge with no expectation of reward.
Motivated by relatedness — focused on interacting with others and building social connections.
Motivated by autonomy — values the freedom to explore, create, and act without external control.
Motivated by competence — seeks progress by mastering difficult tasks and overcoming challenges.
Motivated by extrinsic rewards — driven to complete activities to collect points, badges, and prizes.
Motivated by change — tests the system's boundaries to force improvements or modifications.

fields.title: Player-driven / customization
fields.hint: Select what players can shape directly, from how they look to how they play.

fields.title: Game-driven adaptive systems
fields.hint: Systems that react to a player's current session — adjusting in real time based on how they're playing right now, with no history required.

options.info: The game scales challenge based on performance
Levels, quests, or loot generated based on player behavior or preferences
Story adapts to the user's choices

fields.title: Data-driven / algorithmic personalization
fields.hint: Systems that use accumulated player data (across sessions or players) to shape what an individual sees, is offered, or is matched with.

options.info: Suggests content (missions, cosmetics, events) based on a player's play history.
Groups players by play style to tailor content or onboarding per group.
Delivers personalized offers, notifications, or events based on engagement patterns.
Pairs players using accumulated data like skill, latency, or behavior history — not just current lobby state.

sections.title: Gameful Core
sections.description: This is where the actual game lives — the loops that repeat, the mechanics that drive them, and how players move forward over time.
sections.summary: Game rules and loops, Mechanics, Progression

groups.title: Game rules
groups.description: Lay out the core rules of your system — the constraints and logic that make everything else possible.

groups.title: Gamification & Mechanics
groups.description: Pick a category, select the game elements you're using within it, and describe the mechanics behind each element.

groups.title: Progression
groups.description: Define how the player advances and grows over time

groups.title: Modality
groups.description: Choose how players interact with each other during play.

groups.title: Timing
groups.description: Choose whether players need to be active at the same time, or can participate independently, on their own schedule.

fields.placeholder: e.g. Players earn 1 point per completed task, lose points if a task is skipped 3 days in a row, and can't advance to the next level until they've completed all core tasks in the current one.

fields.title: Game loops
fields.hint: Configure how each time-scale loop works.
fields.description: The basic action a player repeats every few seconds to a couple of minutes. It's the fundamental verb of the game.
fields.popupIntro: The core loop has to feel good on its own, over and over, because the player will do it thousands of times. If this loop isn't satisfying, no amount of long-term progression will save the game.

fields.label: Describe the smallest meaningful sequence of player actions that repeats during ordinary gameplay.
fields.placeholder:
[Action 1] → [Action 2] → [Action 3]
Duration: [seconds/minutes]

fields.label: What immediate result does the player receive, and how does the game communicate it?
fields.placeholder:
Player does: [action]
System produces: [outcome]
Player perceives: [feedback]

fields.label: After receiving the result, what meaningful choice does the player make before repeating or changing the loop?
fields.placeholder:
Result: [outcome]
Player chooses between: [A] / [B] / [C]
Trade-off: [risk, cost, time, reward, information]
Next loop changes because: [consequence]

fields.description: The larger structure that gives the short loop purpose over minutes, hours, or the whole game. It's built from many repetitions of the short loop and typically involves progression, rewards, or strategic decisions.
fields.popupIntro: Describe how repeated gameplay leads to long-term progress, changes the player's future possibilities, and creates the next reason to play.

fields.label: What does the player work toward across multiple sessions, and what concrete milestone marks progress?
fields.placeholder:
Repeated Core Loops produce: [progress/resource]
Long-term goal: [goal]
Milestone: [observable achievement]
Expected timeframe: [time period]

fields.key: Long loop · Change in future play
fields.label: How does reaching the milestone change future play?
fields.placeholder:
Milestone: [achievement]
Unlocks or changes: [system/content/capability]
Core Loop now differs because: [specific change]
New strategic possibility: [possibility]

fields.label: After the milestone, what new goal, challenge, social context, or unresolved desire motivates the player to re-enter the Core Loop?
fields.placeholder:
New ambition: [goal]
Why it matters: [player motivation]
Return trigger: [what brings the player back]
The next cycle is different because: [difference]

fields.label: Attach a sketch or diagram of your loop

options.info: Elements that give the player feedback on how they are doing: points, levels, progression, status, achievements.
Elements based on interaction between players: competition, cooperation, reputation, social pressure.
Elements about the player as an individual: novelty, objectives, puzzles, renovation, sensation.
Elements that tie the experience to a story or context: narrative, storytelling.
Elements tied to the environment the game creates: chance, imposed choice, economy, rarity, time pressure.

options.info: Progress that persists between runs or sessions, even when a single attempt ends.
The player chooses between different paths, each leading to different content.
No fixed end point: players set their own goals and keep progressing.
A central hub from which the player reaches separate areas or missions and then returns.
The progression path is generated by the system instead of being fixed in advance.
Progress happens in repeating cycles, such as seasons or runs, that reset and start again.
Difficulty stays flat for a while and then jumps up, for example at the start of a new level.
Different paths have different difficulty, and the player picks one.

fields.label: Describe the structure of progression in your project:

options.description: Solo experience. Simpler infrastructure, personal focus.
Real-time collaboration toward shared goals.
Teams cooperate internally, but the teams compete against each other.
Real-time competition. Requires matchmaking.
Players do not need to act at the same time; interaction happens across different time frames or turns.
Players act at the same time, so the interaction depends on real-time coordination.

sections.title: Feedback and Evaluation
sections.description: Close the loop: define how the system communicates with players, then how you'll know if it's working. Work through these in order — each answer builds on the last.

itemFields.title: In which part of the process do you want to provide feedback?
What do you prefer to communicate to the user?
itemFields.placeholder: e.g. You were spotted because you ran across a noisy surface…

itemFields.title: What is the feedback typology?
What is the feedback content?
itemFields.placeholder: e.g. A red detection icon fills above the enemy's head, with a short alert stinger

itemFields.title: What is the most suitable timing?
What is the best modality?
What is the best game element that can support feedback?
Feedback presentation:
itemFields.placeholder: e.g. Top-right corner, 400ms fade-in, holds 2s, fades before HUD returns to idle state

itemFields.title: Feedback implementation:
itemFields.placeholder: e.g. Fires from DetectionSystem.onSpotted(); suppress if player is already in combat state

sections.title: Technical requirements
sections.description: Ground your design in what's actually feasible to build — the platforms, engine, and constraints your team is working within.

groups.title: Platforms
groups.description: Select your target platforms — each one comes with its own constraints on your design.

groups.title: Engine and technology stack
groups.description: Define your engine and technology stack; your choice of architecture dictates your production constraints.

groups.title: Runtime and controls
groups.description: Define where and how your game runs, and what players use to control it — this shapes both performance and what mechanics are possible.

groups.title: Display, audio, haptics
groups.description: Define how players interact physically with your system and note any accessibility options you're supporting.

groups.title: Performance budgets
groups.description: Set concrete numbers now, so you're not redesigning around them later.

groups.title: Data, save and online
groups.description: Describe how progress is stored and recovered — lost progress is the fastest way to lose a player.

groups.title: External SDKs and integrations
groups.description: List every third-party SDK you depend on, so each risk is visible before it becomes a problem.

groups.title: Content pipeline
groups.description: Describe your production tools and conventions, so ambitious content stays realistic to produce.

groups.title: Technical risks
groups.description: Log technical unknowns as they come up — untracked risk is what causes late surprises.
